# AI Evaluator Forum and the AEF-1 standard

- Websites: https://aievaluatorforum.org ; standard: https://www.aef.one (redirects to https://www.aef.one/aef-one.pdf)
- Fetched: 2026-10-19. Raw copies: `/data/haokun_test/neurico/safety_kb/sources/ai-evaluator-forum/` (PDF + pdftotext, forum pages).

## What it is
"A network of organizations that conduct independent, third-party evaluations of AI systems" that "shares methods, aligns on professional norms, and informs standards and policy work". Not a legal entity; relies on voluntary participation. Chair: Conrad Stosz (Transluce); Senior Advisor: Patricia Paskov. "Membership is limited to organizations that conduct and publish rigorous independent technical evaluations" of general-purpose AI systems in the public interest. Members listed 2026-10-19: AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute), Collective Intelligence Project, Meridian Labs, METR, Princeton Holistic Agent Leaderboard, RAND, SecureBio, Transluce ("More members coming soon"). Founding date not stated: UNVERIFIED.

## AEF-1: Minimum Operating Conditions for Independent Third Party AI Evaluations (Version 1, updated 2025-12-04)
Authors: Stosz, Elmgren (Transluce); Foster, Chen, Righetti, Barnes, Painter (METR); Balston, McGregor, Werner, Brundage (AVERI); Donoughe, Nedungadi, Götting (SecureBio); Paskov (Oxford Martin AIGI); Kapoor, Narayanan (Princeton); Schwettmann, Steinhardt (Transluce/MIT/Berkeley); Bommasani, Reich (Stanford); Homewood (GovAI); Siddharth, Lalani (CIP); Teague (Meridian Labs); Sevilla (Epoch AI).

Scope (sec. 2, verbatim): "an initial voluntary standard that evaluators can use to demonstrate how they achieved a baseline set of operating conditions for the independence, access, and transparency of a particular third-party evaluation." It "does not address the many critical methodological considerations for conducting scientifically valid AI evaluations" and focuses on evaluations "where third parties maintain the freedom to define the evaluation's methodology", distinguishing "independent audit" from "verification or validation" of a provider's own evaluation. Compliance is shown by publishing the Appendix A checklist with the results; unmet items must be justified.

Five principles with requirements (R) and recommendations (Rec), condensed from sec. 4:
1. **Sufficient Access and Resources**: 1.1 (R) technical access sufficient for the characteristic evaluated: at minimum "open-ended black-box access (via a web UI, an API or both)"; also scaffolding, safeguard exemptions ("reliably evaluating the worst-case scenarios for misuse of dangerous capabilities generally requires access to a model version where mitigations ... are minimized"), intermediate states ("model activations and reasoning traces"), fine-tuning, weights (for open-weight releases), tools, user data. 1.2 (Rec) provider shares system identification, model spec/system prompt, training and test-set information, elicitation know-how, internal results, known reward hacking/contamination, vulnerabilities, "information that might contradict the evaluation result". 1.3 (R) compute for multiple runs and exploration. 1.4 (R) adequate time: "at least 20 business days are often necessary ... when assessing substantially novel systems" (aligned with the EU Code of Practice Appendix 3.4; METR's GPT-5 evaluation "took three weeks"). 1.5 (Rec) legal safe harbor for in-scope actions, "without fear of adverse legal action".
2. **Minimized Conflicts of Interest**: 2.1 (R) no results-contingent compensation. 2.2 (R) provider holds no voting/large share stake and controls no board seats. 2.3 (R) a published COI policy (reporting, recusal, funding restrictions) applied to the evaluation. 2.4 (R) disclosure when paid by the provider or its competitors, when "a meaningful fraction" of funding comes from a provider/its employees/competitors, when equity is held either way, or when staff also work for a provider (as employee, contractor, board member or advisor). 2.5 (R) recusal of anyone with direct equity in the provider (index funds excluded; support staff excluded). 2.6 (Rec) disclose separate agreements that affect independence.
3. **Analytic Autonomy**: 3.1 (Rec) flexibility to define which properties to evaluate (warns against narrow scoping, e.g. "mental health" reduced to suicidal ideation). 3.2 (R) autonomy over methods: metrics (best-of-N, pass@k), elicitation and scaffolding, jailbreaking, scoring rubrics. 3.3 (Rec) evaluator runs the evaluation via direct access rather than through provider staff. 3.4 (R) editorial control over characterisation, evidence, relation to red lines, baselines, scope limits, access limits, and "the general nature of any redactions".
4. **Transparent Methods and Results**: 4.1 (R) enough methodological detail for independent review; may withhold test data but must release representative examples; limit infohazards per a disclosure policy. 4.2 (Rec) upfront disclosure rights to intended audiences incl. the provider's board/safety board and regulators. 4.3 (Rec) audiences not narrowed based on results; disclosure to internal governance proceeds even if the model is not deployed. 4.4 (Rec) no misrepresentation, including using "partial results ... as evidence of a system's capabilities or risks without making the full scope ... available". 4.5 (Rec) no content-based delay. 4.6 (R) "The system provider did not have authority to redact results to conceal concerning findings"; redaction only for privacy, ethics, trade secrets, infohazards or factual accuracy about terms. 4.7 (Rec) a redaction disclaimer stating whether authorities were exercised and what was redacted.
5. **Protection of Sensitive Information**: 5.1 (R) provider permission before releasing results based on non-public information or systems. 5.2 (Rec) evaluation integrity: provider must not "view, retain, share, use, or train on" held-out evaluation data without written consent; canaries; cooperation against overfitting, reward hacking, sandbagging (aligned with EU CoP Appendix 3.5). 5.3 (R) evaluator protects confidential information (NDAs, access controls, cybersecurity; withholding results on unreleased systems until release). 5.4 (R, per Transluce's policy reference) a published responsible-disclosure policy for vulnerabilities and infohazards.

## Adoption (from https://aievaluatorforum.org/initiatives/minimum-operating-conditions)
- Transluce: Mental Health Evaluation (Aug 2026) included the checklist and disclosed operating conditions; Transluce's Independence and Transparency Policy (updated 2026-08-27) and Responsible Disclosure Policy are written to satisfy AEF-1 items 2.3 and 5.4.
- METR: Frontier Risk Report (May 2026) included the AEF-1 reporting checklist.
- SecureBio: GPT-6 Astra pre-release biosecurity assessment (Sept 2026) included the checklist; "uses AEF-1 as a foundation for its organizational principles" (consistent with https://securebio.org/ai/principles/).
- European AI Office "endorsed key AEF-1 provisions as a way for providers to comply with the independence provisions of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice" (forum page; EU AI Office primary statement not fetched: UNVERIFIED).
- The standard's footnotes map the checklist to EU CoP Safety & Security Measure 7.3(1)(g) and California SB 53 section 22757.12(c)(2)(C).
- "The success of AEF-1 requires adoption by a range of stakeholders, including frontier developers." No lab has formally adopted it in a fetched document (Anthropic's 2026-10-15 tiers and OpenAI's 2026-09-22 principles overlap substantially but do not cite it): UNVERIFIED.

## Why it matters
AEF-1 is the only evaluator-written standard in this knowledge base. It converts the informal credibility signals (COI policy, recusal, no contingent pay, editorial control, redaction disclaimers, security practices, 20-business-day access) into a publishable checklist, and three of the most-trusted evaluators already attach it to reports. For a new lab it is the shortest route to legible credibility.
